prompt: I didn't study much, so I guessed some answers ___ random.
why: "At random" is the fixed phrase for choosing without any plan.

context: A friend is explaining why they missed your call.
prompt: Sorry, my phone was ___ silent, so I didn't hear it ring.
why: We say a phone is "on silent" or "on vibrate". It is a fixed phrase.

prompt: Let's order pizza tonight. It's ___ me this time.
why: "It's on me" means I will pay. It is a common everyday phrase.

context: Two friends are saying goodbye after a trip.
prompt: Let's stay ___ touch. Text me anytime!
why: "Stay in touch" is the fixed phrase for keeping contact with someone.

context: A student is talking about a mistake in an email.
prompt: Sorry about the wrong date. I sent it ___ mistake.
why: "By mistake" means you did it without meaning to. It is a fixed phrase.

context: Two coworkers are talking about a busy day.
prompt: I can't talk now. I'm ___ a hurry to catch my train.
why: We say "in a hurry" for needing to move fast. It is a fixed phrase.

context: A friend is talking about a movie they saw.
prompt: The story was boring, but the music was good, ___ least.
why: "At least" is the fixed phrase for pointing out one good thing.

prompt: Dana has a real talent ___ drawing cartoons.
why: We say "a talent for" something.

prompt: I think the main reason ___ the delay is the bad Wi-Fi.
why: We say "the reason for" something.

prompt: Tom's answer ___ my question was really short.
why: We say "an answer to" a question.

prompt: We need a solution ___ this problem before Friday.
why: "A solution for" (or "to") a problem is correct; "of", "with" and "about" don't work.

prompt: Maya has a lot of respect ___ her teachers.
why: We say "respect for" someone.

prompt: My brother has no interest ___ learning to cook.
why: We say "interest in" something.

prompt: Lior got an increase ___ salary after the review.
why: We say "an increase in" salary, prices or numbers.

context: A parent talks to a teenager.
prompt: I have a lot of trust ___ you, so go ahead and plan the trip.
why: We say "trust in" someone.

context: Two friends talk about a classmate.
prompt: Lena has a real talent ___ drawing, so she's going to art school.
why: We say "a talent for" something.

context: A friend arrives late to dinner.
prompt: Sorry I'm late! The reason ___ the delay was the traffic.
why: We say "the reason for" something.

context: A student asks about a new math class
prompt: I think the answer ___ your question is on page twelve.
why: We say "the answer to" a question.

context: Two coworkers chat in the office kitchen.
prompt: There's been a big increase ___ the price of coffee lately.
why: We say "an increase in" prices, numbers or amounts.

context: Two neighbors chat in the hallway
prompt: Tom and his brother have a really good relationship ___ each other.
why: We say "a relationship with" someone.

context: Two friends are talking about a podcast.
prompt: Have you listened ___ the new episode of that podcast yet?
why: We say "listen to" something. Hebrew speakers often skip the preposition or use another one.

context: A coworker is asking about your weekend plans.
prompt: I'm really looking forward ___ the long weekend.
why: "Look forward to" is a fixed expression. It is followed by the thing you are excited about.

context: Two friends are choosing a restaurant.
prompt: It all depends ___ how much money we want to spend.
why: We say "depend on". The Hebrew-style "depend in" is not correct in English.

context: Maya is talking about her sister's job.
prompt: My sister works ___ a big company downtown.
why: "Work for" a company means you are employed by it.

context: A teacher is talking to a student after class.
prompt: Thanks for waiting. I'm sorry ___ being late again.
why: We say "sorry for" followed by an -ing word when we apologize for something we did.

context: Dan is telling a friend about his new apartment.
prompt: I'm still getting used ___ the noise from the street.
why: "Get used to" something means it slowly becomes normal for you.

context: Two coworkers are chatting at lunch.
prompt: Can you believe it? Tom just laughed ___ my idea in the meeting.
why: We "laugh at" something or someone when we find it funny or silly.

context: Lena is at the bus stop when a friend calls.
prompt: Sorry, I can't talk now. I'm waiting ___ the bus and it's almost here.
why: "Wait for" is the correct form. Hebrew speakers sometimes say "wait to" by mistake.

prompt: My cousin got us concert tickets ___ free.
why: "For free" is a fixed phrase meaning without paying.

prompt: Dan is really good ___ cooking.
why: We say "good at" when talking about a skill.

prompt: My little sister is afraid ___ spiders.
why: "Afraid of" is the fixed phrase for a fear.

prompt: Please don't talk ___ the movie.
why: "During" means while something is happening, like a movie.

prompt: Please don't put nuts in it. I'm allergic ___ them.
why: "Allergic to" is the fixed phrase for an allergy.

prompt: Maya is really interested ___ learning the guitar.
why: We say "interested in" something.

context: Maya is explaining why she was late to the meeting.
prompt: Sorry I'm late, I was stuck ___ traffic for an hour.
why: We say "stuck in traffic". "In" is the fixed preposition for being caught inside a line of cars.

context: Two friends are talking about a new phone.
prompt: I got it ___ sale last week, so it was much cheaper.
why: "On sale" means sold at a lower price. It is a fixed phrase.

context: Dan is texting his sister about her headphones.
prompt: Sorry I broke your headphones. I didn't do it ___ purpose.
why: "On purpose" means done deliberately. The opposite is "by accident".

context: Noa is chatting with a coworker about her trip.
prompt: I booked the whole holiday ___ the internet, and it was really easy.
why: We say "on the internet" and "on the phone". Hebrew speakers often say "in the internet".

context: Tom is rushing out the door when his roommate calls.
prompt: Sorry, I can't talk now. I'm ___ a hurry.
why: "In a hurry" is the fixed phrase for rushing.

context: Lena is asking a friend about a restaurant.
prompt: Is this restaurant good? I've never been here ___ my life.
why: We say "never in my life" to stress something has not happened at any time.

context: Sam is describing his favorite show to a colleague.
prompt: You have to watch it! It's ___ TV every night at nine.
why: Programs are "on TV". Hebrew speakers sometimes say "in the TV".

context: Dana is talking about her neighbors.
prompt: Dana complained ___ the noise all night.
why: We say "complain about" something that annoys us.

prompt: Tom is finally recovering ___ the flu.
why: We say "recover from" an illness.

context: A student is talking to a teacher.
prompt: Please don't accuse me ___ something I didn't do.
why: We say "accuse someone of" doing something wrong.

context: Sam is happy about his test.
prompt: After three tries, Sam finally succeeded ___ passing the driving test.
why: We say "succeed in" doing something.

context: Lena is talking to a friend about work.
prompt: I'm dealing ___ a lot of stress at work right now.
why: "Deal with" something means to handle a problem.

prompt: I need to get rid ___ all these old boxes.
why: "Get rid of" something means to throw it away.

context: Eli's parents have opinions about his looks.
prompt: My parents don't approve ___ my new haircut.
why: We say "approve of" something when we think it is good.

context: Vera is talking about her friend's job.
prompt: My friend Omer specializes ___ travel photography.
why: We say "specialize in" a type of work or subject.

context: Maya is telling a friend about her trip.
prompt: We drove ___ the tunnel and came out right by the beach.
why: "Through" is for going in one side of an enclosed space, like a tunnel, and out the other.

context: Dan is giving directions to a tourist.
prompt: Walk ___ the bridge and the station is on your left.
why: "Across" means from one side of something flat, like a bridge or river, to the other.

context: Tom is talking about his morning routine.
prompt: I usually jump ___ the shower as soon as I wake up.
why: "Into" shows movement from outside to the inside of something, like a shower or a car.

context: Lena is watching her little brother at the playground.
prompt: He climbed ___ the tree and wouldn't come down.
why: "Up" is used for moving to a higher place, like climbing a tree.

context: Rachel is telling her roommate about the neighbor's cat.
prompt: The cat jumped ___ the fence and ran into our yard.
why: "Over" is used for moving above something and reaching the other side, like a fence.
